However, not all synthetic data can adequately reproduce the characteristics of the original data set, as shown by the experience of the Central Bank of Türkiye and Istanbul Technical University. Consistent with this observation, the Central Bank of Malaysia has developed an evaluation framework to assess the quality of synthetic data. This framework measures statistical distance, structural similarity, performance in machine learning tasks and the risk of disclosing sensitive information to produce a composite weighted score for evaluating synthetic data. Finally, collaboration between central banks and other stakeholders involved in the data ecosystem can play a decisive role in advancing generative AI applications. For example, t he BIS Innovation Hub Ellipse Data and Knowledge Platform Community (EDKP) provides a platform for central banks and financial regulators to share source code, pool expertise and jointly develop AI-based supervisory technology solutions supporting financial supervision. Collaboration can also involve actors beyond the c entral bank ing/supervisory community, such as statistical offices, international organisations, academia and the private sector , for example by sharing knowledge, software and co -investment opportunities (IFC (2025a)). 16 IFC Bulletin No 67 Glossary Artificial intelligence (AI): computer systems capable of tasks that normally require human intelligence (FSB (2017)), for instance by inferring how to generate outputs from the inputs they receive (OECD (2024)). It includes applications such as machine learning (ML) and generative AI. AI agents : systems designed to act autonomously, making decisions and taking actions based on their programming and objectives. These systems are capable of performing tasks without constant human intervention. AI-ready data : data that are suitable for consumption by AI systems and models , such as LLMs . K ey dimensions for readiness include quality, interoperability, accessibility and compliance (both ethical and legal). Generative AI: a subset of AI that produces new content, such as text, images, audio or video, based on patterns learned from existing data (or “training data”), usually in response to a user’s prompt. Knowledge base: a repository of information that provides domain -specific or general data to AI models. Knowledge bases can include various data types, including textual documents,

chunks.text: such as text, images, audio or video, based on patterns learned from existing data (or “training data”), usually in response to a user’s prompt. Knowledge base: a repository of information that provides domain -specific or general data to AI models. Knowledge bases can include various data types, including textual documents, which can be used to provide organisation -specific context through techniques such as RAG. Large language models (LLMs): AI models trained on vast amounts of text data with the goal of generating human-like language. These models are designed to perform a wide range of natural language processing tasks, including summaris ing, translating, answering questions and interacting with users. Model Context Protocol (MCP): an open framework and standard that enables the integration of AI systems with selected external software and data sources. Privacy-enhancing and -preserving technologies: technologies to minimise risks of privacy infringement, such as anonymisation, encryption, differential privacy, homomorphic encryption and secure multiparty computation. Retrieval-augmented generation system (RAG) : a technique aimed at improving the quality of generative AI responses by integrating relevant context from pre - defined knowledge sources to each user prompt, offering reliable and well -defined sources for the generation of responses. Small language models (SLMs) : AI models s imilar to LLMs, but with significantly fewer parameters that are trained on less data than LLMs. While their smaller size reduces their capabilities compared with LLMs, SLMs are less computationally intensive and can often serve more specialised roles in specific domains. chunks.text: on Central Bank Statistics (IFC) 18 February 2025, Rome, Italy Good morning, distinguished guests, colleagues, and friends, It is my great pleasure to welcome you all to the 4th Workshop on Data Science in Central Banking organized by the BIS Irving Fisher Committee on Central Bank Statistics (IFC) and hosted by the Bank of Italy. As we gather today, we are reminded of the rapid advancements in data science and its profound impact on central banking. Indeed, t he sheer volume and complexity of financial data now available call for more sophisticated techniques for data management and analysis. This trend is reinforced by the new opportunities opened up by artificial intelligence and machine learning . This workshop is a testimony to our collective commitment to harnessing innovation to enhance central bank’ operations, policy-making, and overall effectiveness. As emphasized in the last 2024 IFCs Annual Report just endorsed by the BIS All Governors a few weeks ago , the current focus on data science and AI supports the broader objective of improving statistical methods and fostering innovation in central banks . Th is IFC report underscores that leveraging new technologies can be instrumental to enhance data quality, improve analytical capabilities, and support evidence -based policymaking. The Report also calls for reviewing the related ongoing initiatives pursued by central banks and for providing a platform for sharing knowledge and best practices. Let me recall that the three previous IFC data science workshops have been dealing with, respectively, (1) machine learning applications; (2) applications and tools in data science; and (3) data access and sharing. This time we will over the next three days delve into the various aspects related to the use of generative AI in central bank activities. We will hear from esteemed exp erts and practitioners who will share their insights and experiences, providing us with valuable knowledge and practical tools to navigate the evolving landscape of data science. I would like first to extend a special welcome to our keynote speaker, Julien Simon, Chief Evangelist at Arcee.ai, who will be discussing the tailoring of small language models for enterprise

I would like first to extend a special welcome to our keynote speaker, Julien Simon, Chief Evangelist at Arcee.ai, who will be discussing the tailoring of small language models for enterprise use cases. His expertise and vision will undoubtedly set the tone for our discussions. Then the sessions of the workshop will cover various critical areas, such as natural language processing tools , AI for summarization and information extraction , supervisory technology , text analysis for market monitoring and monetary policy purposes, and data privacy and anonymization. * * * Let me share with you a few thoughts on these issues: First, the new techniques we will discuss are not only very timely, but they are also essential to leverage data science to address the complex challenges we face in modern central banking. In particular, t he integration of generative AI and advanced data analytics into central banks ’ operations can significantly enhance their ability to make informed decisions, assess economic trends, and work to promote monetary and financial stability. More generally, IT innovation provides brand new perspectives. For instance, open-source software offer numerous benefits supporting official statistics and data analysis, including cost savings, flexibility, and the ability to customi ze solutions to meet specific needs. Another example is that modern data management approaches such as data lakes and data meshes architectures allow for new ways to store, organize, and access data [Note that I said data lakes not “data ponds”, and data m esh not “data mess”!!]. This calls for careful planning and for not blindly following the crowd and fashionable buzz words. The main goal is to concretely help central banks to more effectively leverage their information assets, improve the integration and quality of their data, and support more sophisticated analytical techniques. Second, your presence here today, coming from various jurisdictions all over the world and representing central banks, other public authorities, international organizations, academia and the private sector , underlines the importance of the goal of this workshop

chunks.docTitle: Ifc Bulletin 67 Data Science Central Banking Exploring Generative Ai
chunks.text: the integration and quality of their data, and support more sophisticated analytical techniques. Second, your presence here today, coming from various jurisdictions all over the world and representing central banks, other public authorities, international organizations, academia and the private sector , underlines the importance of the goal of this workshop , which is to showcase concrete projects, share experiences, develop in-house knowledge and also reduce reliance on external service providers. Third, central banks, as producers of official data, have a key role to play to promote the access and dissemination of credible information to various external stakeholders, including other domestic authorities, international institutions, academia, and the general public. But better data is also key for supporting realtime, evidence-based policymaking in central banks , which increasingly rely on trustworthy data and sophisticated analytical and forecasting capacities to support their decisions. Fourth, the relevance of artificial intelligence for central banks cannot be overstated, as it of fers immense opportunities to enhance productivity, improve decision - making, and foster innovation. In particular, Generative AI has the potential to revolutionize data analysis and interpretation, offering deeper insights and more accurate predictions. For instance, the use of large language models can significantly enhance our ability to process and understand vast amounts of unstructured data, ranging from economic reports to news articles, thereby enabling us to make more informed policy decisions especially in the areas of monetary policy, financial stability, and regulatory oversight. However, and this is my fifth point, GenAI also presents significant challenges and risks. Central banks must navigate issues such as data privacy, security, and ethical considerations. The potential for systemic risks, such as homogenization of information and procyclicality, requires careful management. As central banks increasingly rely on data -driven approaches, it is essential to ensure that sensitive information is protected, and that data is used ethically and responsibly. And my last point is that address ing these challenges calls for developing robust governance frameworks. This is key so that w e can harness the power of AI while mitigating its risks, ensuring that our financial systems remain stable and resilient. At the

This is key so that w e can harness the power of AI while mitigating its risks, ensuring that our financial systems remain stable and resilient. At the same time investing in advanced IT infrastructure and fostering collaboration and coordination as we do today can help to stay abreast of emerging threats and implement best practices. * * * To conclude, this workshop aims to gather a diverse audience of practitioners, specialists, and interested stakeholders from central banks, international organizations, national statistical offices, and beyond. Our primary objective is to highlight ongoing projects and exchange experiences that can help foster in - house expertise and lessen reliance on external service providers. For instance, a number of p rojects that will be presented in the next few days have replicable codes developed with open-source software and can be usefully shared among all interested stakeholders . Moreover, the presentations will enhance our understanding of the opportunities and risks associated with new Generative AI technologies. This is key for central banks willing to navigate the evolving financial landscape and ensure that they are well-positioned to meet future challenges. I therefore encourage you all to actively participate in the sessions, engage with the speakers, and share your own experiences and perspectives. It is through this collaborative spirit that we can truly advance our understanding and application of data science in our field . Before closing, I would like to thank the organizers, speakers, and all participants for your dedication and contributions to this workshop. I am confident that our time together will be both enlightening and inspiring, and I look forward to the fruitful discussions and innovative ideas that will emerge. Thank you, and welcome once again to the 4th Workshop on Data Science in Central Banking. chunks.text: # Rural Business Advisory Expert Training Guide ## From Zero Knowledge to Expert *Designed for training AI chatbots and human advisors in rural business advisory services* --- ### 1. Purpose and Audience This guide provides a structured curriculum to develop expertise in rural business advisory. It synthesizes competency frameworks, course outlines, and best practices from international sources (Teagasc, CECRA, GFRAS, SocAg, Wichita State, etc.) into a modular learning path. The content can be used to: - Fine-tune language models for rural advisory chatbots - Train human extension agents, consultants, and agribusiness advisors - Serve as a reference knowledge base for advisory practitioners Target learners: Individuals with no prior advisory experience seeking to become competent rural business advisors capable of supporting farmers, agri-enterprises, and rural communities. --- ### 2. Overview of Rural Business Advisory Rural business advisory is a target‑ and solution‑oriented communicative relationship between advisor and client, geared exclusively to the client’s success. It requires: - **Expert technical knowledge** (farm management, economics, policy, technology) - **Methodological skills** (advisory process design, facilitation, monitoring) - **Communication and social skills** (active listening, questioning, presentation) - **Personal attributes** (self‑reflection, ethics, continuous learning, intercultural competence) Advisors operate in complex environments where trust, relationships, and local context often outweigh pure technical advice. Modern advisors must also navigate digital tools, data analytics, and innovation while maintaining strong interpersonal competencies. --- ### 3. Core Competency Areas Derived from Teagasc Competency Set – Business and Technology Advisor, CECRA Guidelines, and GFRAS RAS Curriculum Development. | Competency Area | Description | Key Elements | |----------------|-------------|--------------| | **Technical Knowledge** | Dissemination and application of expert knowledge to enhance farm and enterprise performance. | Up‑to‑date knowledge of advisory areas; practical application; value‑adding focus; market trends; research integration. | | **Work & Project Organisation** | Planning, organising, and managing advisory assignments and projects. | Goal setting; work planning; use of templates; performance data analysis; option generation. | | **Commercial Orientation** | Advisor’s ability to help clients make sound commercial decisions and achieve viable returns. | Commercial analysis; value‑added focus; entrepreneurial skill development; risk assessment; market opportunity identification. | | **Communication, Education & Knowledge

| Goal setting; work planning; use of templates; performance data analysis; option generation. | | **Commercial Orientation** | Advisor’s ability to help clients make sound commercial decisions and achieve viable returns. | Commercial analysis; value‑added focus; entrepreneurial skill development; risk assessment; market opportunity identification. | | **Communication, Education & Knowledge Transfer** | Informative, relevant, timely advice using appropriate methods; develops client thinking. | Multi‑media communication; group facilitation; tool/template design; colleague knowledge sharing; field notes archiving. | | **Continuous Professional Development (CPD)** | Keeping abreast of leading trends, thinking, and skills to maintain credibility. | Regular knowledge/skill updates; networking; coaching/mentoring; PDP participation; environmental scanning; learning from colleagues. | | **Methodological Skills** (CECRA) | Structured approach to advisory processes. | Relationship building; task clarification; advisory models; project management; moderation; visualization; process guidance; change monitoring; problem/conflict solving; adult education management. | | **Communication & Social Skills** (CECRA) | Effective interaction within teams and with clients. | Cooperation; networking; conversational basics; esteem; questioning; active listening; relationship formation; information literacy; high‑profile knowledge transfer; criticism acceptance; conflict handling. | | **Personal Skills** (CECRA) | Intrapersonal and interpersonal effectiveness. | Analytical faculties; personal appearance; self‑organisation; work techniques; goal‑oriented working; willingness to learn/change; intercultural competence; innovative thinking; recognition of limits; self‑care; self‑reflection; work reflection. | --- ### 4. Glossary of Selected Terms - **Advisory**: A target‑ and solution‑oriented communicative relationship aimed at client success. - **Extension**: Traditionally technology‑transfer focused; now often includes advisory functions. - **Consultancy**: Expert advice for a fee, often problem‑specific. - **Rural Advisory Services (RAS)**: Encompasses extension, advisory, and consultancy for rural livelihood improvement. - **SMART Skills**: Skills for Marketing and Rural Transformation – a competency model for farmers and advisors. - **CECRA**: Certificate for European Consultants in Rural Areas – a competency‑based advisory qualification. - **GFRAS**: Global Forum for Rural Advisory Services – sets good practices for RAS. - **Continuous Professional Development (CPD)**: Ongoing learning to maintain and enhance professional competence. - **Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA)**: Approaches for involving locals in analysis, planning, and action. - **BATNA**: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. - **GROW Model**: Goal, Reality, Options, Way forward – a coaching framework. --- ### 10. Rural entrepreneurship in India has emerged as a critical driver of inclusive economic growth, particularly in the wake of government initiatives aimed at fostering self-employment and enterprise development in non-farm sectors. The Start-up Village Entrepreneurship Programme (SVEP), launched in 2016 as a sub-scheme of the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), has been instrumental in supporting rural entrepreneurs by providing financial assistance, institutional support, business management training, and mentoring. By June 2026, SVEP had supported over 4.32 lakh rural enterprises across the country, with a strong focus on social inclusion, as approximately 86% of entrepreneurs belong to Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe, Minority, and Other Backward Communities.

 
The programme operates through Community Resource Persons – Enterprise Promotion (CRP-EPs), who are selected from Self Help Group (SHG) households and provide mentoring, training, and credit facilitation to up to 50 enterprises each. At least 90% of CRP-EPs are drawn from SHG households, with women constituting a minimum of 60% of the cadre. This structure ensures that support is deeply embedded within the community, leveraging existing social capital and trust networks to facilitate enterprise creation and sustainability.

 
SVEP's impact extends beyond mere enterprise creation; it has been shown to improve confidence, livelihood security, and household well-being among beneficiaries. Entrepreneurs report increased savings, reinvestment in their businesses, and enhanced social standing within their communities. Many households have experienced better education, nutrition, health, and sanitation outcomes as a direct result of increased income and empowerment through entrepreneurship.

 
Another significant initiative is the ASPIRE scheme (A Scheme for Promotion of Innovation, Rural Industries and Entrepreneurship) under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME). ASPIRE promotes innovation and entrepreneurship in agro-rural sectors through a network of Livelihood Business Incubators (LBIs) that provide skill development, mentoring, and incubation support. The scheme helps aspiring entrepreneurs acquire the skills and confidence needed to transform ideas into viable enterprises, particularly in sectors such as food processing, handicrafts, and other value-added activities.

Women's entrepreneurship in rural India has been a focal point of several government programs. The NITI Aayog's Women Entrepreneurship Platform (WEP) serves as a one-stop shop for women entrepreneurs, offering support in areas such as funding, mentorship, and networking. Reports indicate that women-owned enterprises constitute about 20% of proprietary MSMEs, with a noticeable urban-rural divide. Initiatives like the Mahila Kisan Sashaktikaran Pariyojana (MKSP) and the Support to Training and Employment Programme for Women (STEP) aim to enhance women's participation in agriculture and allied sectors.

 
The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) plays a pivotal role in promoting rural entrepreneurship through its Farm Sector Promotion Fund (FSPF) and Watershed Development Fund (WDF). NABARD supports Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs), which have emerged as a key model for collectivizing smallholder farmers to achieve economies of scale in input procurement, value addition, and market access. As of December 2024, nearly 44,000 FPOs had been registered in India, supported by central schemes such as the Formation and Promotion of 10,000 FPOs (CSS) with a budget outlay of ■6,865 crore.

 
FPOs facilitate better price realization, reduce transaction costs, and enable members to access credit, technology, and markets more effectively. They act as intermediaries between individual farmers and larger buyers, processors, and exporters. The success of FPOs often hinges on strong support from intermediary organisations such as NGOs, agribusinesses, and financial institutions, which provide capacity-building, market linkages, and financial services.

Challenges to rural entrepreneurship include limited access to affordable credit, inadequate infrastructure (such as power, water, and transportation), skill gaps, and socio-cultural barriers. Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) represent a collective action model that enables smallholder farmers to overcome challenges such as fragmented landholdings, limited bargaining power, and high transaction costs. By pooling resources, FPOs can achieve economies of scale in input procurement, access better technology, and engage in value addition activities such as processing and packaging.

 
The success of FPOs depends on several factors, including strong governance, effective leadership, access to credit and markets, and the ability to manage internal conflicts. Intermediary organisations such as NGOs, consultants, and financial institutions play a vital role in providing technical assistance, capacity-building, and market linkages. For instance, digital agri-tech firms like DeHaat and AgNext offer FPOs real-time advisory, weather forecasts, and market intelligence, enabling better decision-making.

Value chain interventions are essential for increasing the share of value captured by rural producers. These schemes aim to increase productivity, reduce post-harvest losses, and enhance the competitiveness of horticulture produce in domestic and international markets.

 
The food processing sector offers significant opportunities for rural entrepreneurship, particularly in areas such as grain milling, oil extraction, and ready-to-eat foods. Schemes like the Pradhan Mantri Formalisation of Micro Food Processing Enterprises Scheme (PMFME) provide financial assistance, training, and handholding support to micro food processing enterprises, enabling them to upgrade technology, improve hygiene standards, and access markets.

 
PMFME targets individuals, Self Help Groups, Farmer Producer Organisations, and cooperatives, with a special focus on women and SC/ST entrepreneurs. The scheme offers credit-linked subsidies of up to 35% of the project cost, with a maximum ceiling of ■10 lakh per unit. By March 2026, PMFME had sanctioned thousands of units across the country, contributing to the formalization and growth of the micro food processing sector.

Paragraph 1:
Rural entrepreneurship in India has emerged as a critical driver of inclusive economic growth, particularly in the wake of government initiatives aimed at fostering self-employment and enterprise development in non-farm sectors. The Start-up Village Entrepreneurship Programme (SVEP), launched in 2016 as a sub-scheme of the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM), has been instrumental in supporting rural entrepreneurs by providing financial assistance, institutional support, business management training, and mentoring. By June 2026, SVEP had supported over 4.32 lakh rural enterprises across the country, with a strong focus on social inclusion, as approximately 86% of entrepreneurs belong to Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe, Minority, and Other Backward Communities.

Paragraph 2:
The programme operates through Community Resource Persons – Enterprise Promotion (CRP-EPs), who are selected from Self Help Group (SHG) households and provide mentoring, training, and credit facilitation to up to 50 enterprises each. At least 90% of CRP-EPs are drawn from SHG households, with women constituting a minimum of 60% of the cadre. This structure ensures that support is deeply embedded within the community, leveraging existing social capital and trust networks to facilitate enterprise creation and sustainability.

Paragraph 3:
SVEP's impact extends beyond mere enterprise creation; it has been shown to improve confidence, livelihood security, and household well-being among beneficiaries. Entrepreneurs report increased savings, reinvestment in their businesses, and enhanced social standing within their communities. Many households have experienced better education, nutrition, health, and sanitation outcomes as a direct result of increased income and empowerment through entrepreneurship.

The scheme helps aspiring entrepreneurs acquire the skills and confidence needed to transform ideas into viable enterprises, particularly in sectors such as food processing, handicrafts, and other value-added activities.

Reports indicate that women-owned enterprises constitute about 20% of proprietary MSMEs, with a noticeable urban-rural divide. Initiatives like the Mahila Kisan Sashaktikaran Pariyojana (MKSP) and the Support to Training and Employment Programme for Women (STEP) aim to enhance women's participation in agriculture and allied sectors.

The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) plays a pivotal role in promoting rural entrepreneurship through its Farm Sector Promotion Fund (FSPF) and Watershed Development Fund (WDF). NABARD supports Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs), which have emerged as a key model for collectivizing smallholder farmers to achieve economies of scale in input procurement, value addition, and market access. As of December 2024, nearly 44,000 FPOs had been registered in India, supported by central schemes such as the Formation and Promotion of 10,000 FPOs (CSS) with a budget outlay of ₹6,865 crore.

They act as intermediaries between individual farmers and larger buyers, processors, and exporters. The success of FPOs often hinges on strong support from intermediary organisations such as NGOs, agribusinesses, and financial institutions, which provide capacity-building, market linkages, and financial services.

Skill gaps in areas such as business management, digital literacy, and technical know-how can limit the ability of entrepreneurs to innovate and compete. Vocational training programs, Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs), and Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) offer opportunities for skill upgradation. Additionally, mentorship programs and peer learning networks can facilitate knowledge sharing and capacity building.

Paragraph 49:
Market access is often hampered by lack of information about demand, prices, and buyer preferences. Initiatives such as agricultural market reforms, the development of online trading platforms, and the promotion of contract farming can help farmers and entrepreneurs realize better prices. Export promotion councils and trade facilitation measures can also assist in accessing international markets.

Paragraph 50:
Policy coherence and convergence across different ministries and departments are essential to avoid duplication and ensure synergistic impact. For instance, alignment between the Ministry of Rural Development (for SVEP), the Ministry of MSME (for ASPIRE and MUDRA), the Ministry of Agriculture (for FPOs and value chains), and the Ministry of Skill Development (for training) can create a more integrated support system.

Paragraph 51:
The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted both the vulnerabilities and the resilience of rural enterprises. While many businesses faced disruptions due to lockdowns and supply chain breaks, others adapted by shifting to online sales, producing essential goods such as masks and sanitizers, and leveraging local networks. The experience underscored the importance of digital readiness and diversification of income sources.

Paragraph 52:
Looking ahead, the integration of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, and the Internet of Things (IoT) holds potential for transforming rural entrepreneurship. AI can provide predictive analytics for demand forecasting, blockchain can enhance supply chain transparency, and IoT can enable smart agriculture and real-time monitoring of livestock and crops.

Paragraph 53:

Public-private partnerships in research and technology transfer can accelerate the adoption of emerging technologies in rural areas.

Paragraph 54:
In summary, rural entrepreneurship in India is supported by a robust ecosystem of government schemes, financial institutions, non-governmental organizations, and private sector actors. The Start-up Village Entrepreneurship Programme, ASPIRE, MUDRA, FPO promotion, and value chain interventions collectively address the multidimensional challenges faced by rural entrepreneurs. By continuing to strengthen these interventions, address implementation gaps, and foster innovation, India can unlock the entrepreneurial potential of its rural population and drive inclusive and sustainable growth.

Paragraph 55:
The collective impact of these efforts is evident in the millions of rural enterprises that have been created, the incomes generated, and the employment opportunities provided. As rural entrepreneurs continue to innovate and adapt, they contribute not only to economic development but also to social empowerment, environmental stewardship, and the preservation of traditional knowledge and crafts.

Paragraph 56:
Policy makers, practitioners, and stakeholders must remain committed to learning from experience, adapting to changing contexts, and scaling up successful models. With sustained effort and a shared vision, rural entrepreneurship can become a cornerstone of India's journey towards becoming a $5 trillion economy by 2027-28, ensuring that growth is inclusive, equitable, and beneficial to all sections of society.
